record.body:
This research programme began in January 2026 from a desire to understand the human spirit, soul, and body more deeply than existing accounts allowed. As the work developed, a conviction settled: an honest account of the human inner being is incomplete without a parallel account of the Holy Spirit. The two stand in relation to one another — the human inner life is shaped, inhabited, and addressed by the Spirit throughout Scripture — and neither can be studied at depth while leaving the other undefined.

The mission that followed was straightforward in statement and substantial in commitment: take a deep dive. Investigate both subjects on their own terms; let Scripture lead the evidence; hold the enquiry open long enough to reach findings rather than assumptions. The commitment produced two elaborate documents, each a collection of deep-dive studies in its own right:

- Framework A — *The Holy Spirit: Origin, Nature, Work, Character, and Interaction. A Five-Thousand-Year Investigation from Genesis to the Present Day.* An investigation of the Holy Spirit across the full biblical canon and beyond it into the receiving tradition.
- Framework B — *Spirit, Soul, and Body: The Composition of Human Beings. A Comprehensive Biblical and Scientific Investigation.* An investigation of the human person as Scripture describes the composition, and as scientific enquiry approaches the same subject from a different direction.
record.heading: Mission
record.author: researcher

record.body:
The advent of the Framework A and Framework B documents did not close the work. By February 2026, with both studies in a readable state, it had become clear that each would benefit from further research and refinement — in style and in depth. Further reading into Framework B's subject made the sharper point: the study had only touched the surface of what the soul actually consists of. A cursory overview counted some twenty-eight distinct characteristics — an order of magnitude short of what a careful treatment of the biblical evidence plainly contains.

That shortfall triggered a deliberate extension of scope: an in-depth exploration of the soul, set within the wider frame of the inner being so that soul, spirit, and body could be treated in their actual relation rather than in isolation. A thorough collation of Scripture's inner-being vocabulary was assembled — approximately two hundred English words, mapped to their Hebrew and Greek originals. That registry became the scope of the present focus of the programme. Every word in it is in scope; every word outside it is out of scope. The registry is the boundary, and the boundary is the basis on which everything downstream — verse selection, term classification, dimensional analysis, cross-registry synthesis — is defined.
record.heading: Scope
record.author: researcher

record.body:
The Soul Word Analysis Programme is the direct continuation of the work the two Frameworks began. It takes the registry of inner-being words — scope defined — and subjects each one to systematic examination: what the term means across its Hebrew and Greek originals, how it occurs across its verses, what contexts the occurrences share, what it contributes to the larger account of the inner person. The programme's intellectual frame is Framework B's; its scale and discipline are new. The earlier work was comprehensive and synthetic; this programme is corpus-level and analytical.

The unit of work is the word. For each word in the registry, the programme builds a complete analytical record — from the Strong's-level term data through the verse inventory and the occurrence contexts, into the characteristic patterns the verses reveal, through to a written word study and, beyond that, cross-registry synthesis. The work runs in phases. Each phase has a defined input, a defined output, and an inflection point at which the word is ready to move to the next phase. A word that has not satisfied the inflection point stays where it is; no phase is skipped; no assessment made at one phase is treated as final before the next phase confirms it.

The programme is organised around a two-agent architecture. The research judgement — what a verse is about, how a term functions in context, which dimensions of the inner being the evidence engages, what the written study should say — is held by the analytical agent working with the researcher. The database operations — extraction, classification persistence, patch application, extract production — are held by a separate operational agent. The separation is deliberate: analytical judgement is the programme's scarce resource, and the architecture protects it from the distraction of mechanical work. The two agents interact through structured artefacts — patches and directives — that make every database change reviewable by the researcher before it takes effect.

The programme's outputs have three orders. First-order outputs are the per-word records and written studies produced one word at a time. Second-order outputs are the cross-word syntheses that emerge when groups of words are examined together — clusters of related characteristics, recurrent patterns across the inner-being vocabulary, places where two frameworks of description illuminate each other. Third-order output is the programme-wide account that these syntheses contribute to: an in-depth description of the human inner being as Scripture reveals it, built from the bottom up on the evidence of every word in scope. The present prose corpus is itself part of that third-order work — the self-description that makes the programme's findings readable as a whole.
record.heading: This Inner-Being Programme
record.author: researcher

record.body:
*What are the inner workings of the human being as described in Scripture — characterising and grouping the inner characteristics, mapping their interrelationships, describing the spirit-soul-body boundary, and documenting the relational interfaces with God, other humans, and other spiritual beings?*

The observation framework defines the complete scope of analytical enquiry for every inner-being characteristic studied in the programme. It has two layers. The **first tier** defines the major analytical domains — the areas that together constitute a complete characterisation of any inner-being characteristic. There are eight first-tier domains: T0 through T7. Not every domain will be richly populated for every characteristic — some domains will be silent for a given word. The first tier defines what could be explored; the evidence determines what is found. The **second tier** defines the constituent components within each first-tier domain — the specific questions and elements that analytical work within that domain addresses. The second tier is under development and is documented separately. The framework functions as a discipline of consistent and complete enquiry. Applied to every word in the programme's scope, it ensures that no area of the inner being is systematically missed, and that findings across words are produced on the same analytical footing.

**Epistemological basis.** The framework rests on an epistemological basis that applies uniformly across all tiers. **Scripture is the primary and governing source.** What Scripture says about a characteristic within any tier is the finding. If Scripture is silent on an aspect of any tier, that silence is noted — it is not filled by inference or from other sources. **Original language analysis** — Hebrew and Greek lexical and semantic study — is the primary evidential tool. It is a sub-discipline of the Scripture source, not a separate source. **Human science frameworks** — psychology, moral philosophy, developmental psychology, sociology, anthropology, linguistics, hermeneutics — serve as interpretive lenses and light sanity checks. They illuminate and organise what Scripture describes. They help ensure that the reading of the evidence is coherent and complete. They do not add content to any tier. The scope of human science engagement is selective and practical — not exhaustive. A full human science treatment of any single tier represents a lifetime of scholarly work for specialists. The programme's engagement is bounded: it draws on human science frameworks where they help ensure completeness and coherence; it does not attempt to replicate specialist scholarship in each discipline.

**T0 — Divine Image and Created Design.** The purposive frame of the programme. T0 holds the foundational question of why this characteristic exists and what it reveals about the human person as image-bearer of God. T0 is the purposive envelope within which all the analytical tiers operate. It does not ask how a characteristic works, where it lives, or how it connects to other characteristics. It asks why it exists — what it reveals about the nature of God whose image the person bears, and what created purpose it serves in the human person. The human person is made in the image of God — *imago Dei*. Every inner-being characteristic exists within that frame. The characteristics the programme studies are not merely psychological or relational phenomena; they are constitutive features of image-bearing persons. T0 examines what each characteristic reveals about the divine nature it images and the created purpose it serves. T0 operates at two levels. At the level of the individual characteristic, it asks: what does this characteristic reveal about the nature of God? What created purpose does it serve in the human person? How does it express God's own character reflected in the image-bearer? At the level of the programme as a whole, T0 asks: what does this entire constellation of inner-being characteristics reveal about what it means to be made in the image of God — what is the human being designed to be, do, and become? The individual-characteristic level of T0 is addressed in Session B. The programme-level question is the governing concern of Session D. T0 is present at every stage of the programme, but it comes fully into its own in Session D, where the characteristics studied across the programme are held together and the integrating question of the divine image is examined in the aggregate. Sexuality finds its primary home in T0. The male-female construct in Scripture is not merely biological or constitutional — it is used typologically throughout Scripture as a language for expressing relational, creative, and covenantal realities that transcend the biological. God describes himself as Father; the church is the bride of Christ; the covenant between God and his people is imaged in the marriage bond. These are not incidental analogies. They are Scripture's deliberate deployment of the created reality of sexuality to point toward and participate in the structure of the divine-human relationship. T0 is where that significance is examined. *Scope boundary: T0 does not ask where a characteristic is located, through which faculties it operates, or how it connects to other characteristics. Those questions belong in T2–T7. T0 asks why the characteristic exists and what it reveals about the divine image and created design.*

**T1 — Definition.** A definition in the making. T1 establishes the current best description of a characteristic — what it is called, what kind of inner-being phenomenon it appears to be, and what it is not. T1 establishes the current best description of a characteristic before the analytical tiers begin. It has three elements: Name, Kind, and Boundary. All three are written from knowledge at hand at the point of first encounter. All three are explicitly held open — reframeable as the research that follows produces findings. T1 is revisited at the conclusion of the full analysis, and the description is updated to reflect what has been found. The definition grows in precision and depth as the research progresses. T1 is therefore visited twice: at the beginning to orient the enquiry, and at the end to receive what the research has revealed. **Name** — what is this characteristic called, and what does the name itself signal? This includes the primary Hebrew and Greek terms and what their root meanings reveal at the definitional level. Name is the most stable element of T1 — it does not change, though its significance may deepen as analysis proceeds. **Kind** — what kind of inner-being phenomenon does this characteristic appear to be at the point of first encounter? Kind is not a category label applied from outside — it is a description that encapsulates the characteristic within the constitutional location it occupies, the faculties it engages, and the impact it produces in the person. It is written as a working description from current knowledge and rewritten after the analytical tiers have completed their work. The programme's dimension vocabulary provides reference categories useful for pattern recognition and comparison — but Kind is not reducible to a dimension assignment. It is a descriptive synthesis that the dimension vocabulary may inform but does not constrain. The dimension vocabulary itself is open: it represents the programme's current best reading of the kinds of inner-being phenomena Scripture describes, and it is subject to revision as the analytical work deepens. **Boundary** — what is this characteristic not? The structural opposite of the characteristic is identified and described. The boundary defines the characteristic by contrast — it sharpens the description by naming what this characteristic stands against or excludes. Like Kind, Boundary is written from current knowledge and is reframeable as research proceeds. *Scope boundary: T1 does not ask where the characteristic is located, through which faculties it operates, how it relates to others, or how it develops. T1 asks only: what is this characteristic, as best as can currently be described?*

**T2 — Constitutional Location and Boundaries.** T2 maps a characteristic onto the constitutional structure of the human person — identifying where it is seated, where it is expressed, and how it moves across constitutional boundaries. Constitutional locations are not physical organs. The body and its structures — including the brain — are the design layer through which the constitutional person interfaces with the physical world. A characteristic may be expressed through the body without being housed there. Cognition is not located in the brain — the brain is the physical connector through which cognition engages the physical world; the cognitive faculty transcends the body and persists beyond it (Scripture shows the dead knowing, remembering, and recognising — Luke 16). The constitutional locations T2 examines are: the spirit (the deepest level of the person and the primary site of encounter with God); the soul (the seat of the faculties and their expression into the characteristics of innermost personal experience); the heart and mind as named subsets of the soul (with other soul subsets held open where the evidence surfaces them); and the body (the physical design layer, with DNA as its design print carried forward generationally, and specific body parts explicitly linked to characteristics in Scripture). When Scripture links a characteristic to a body part, T2 examines the significance of that link — what Scripture is doing by making the connection. The link may be emphatic (giving vividness to a soul-level reality), functional (the body part genuinely participates in the characteristic), expressive (the body gives outward utterance to the inner reality), indicative (the body signals the inner state), or mediating (the body is the channel through which the characteristic enters the person from outside). T2 also examines the direction of the body-characteristic relationship — whether the soul expresses through the body, the body feeds back to the soul, or both — and whether sustained operation of the characteristic leaves a constitutional deposit in the body or its design. *Scope boundary: T2 asks where a characteristic is constitutionally located, where it originates, and what Scripture is doing when it links the characteristic to constitutional elements and body parts. The question of where a characteristic originates — whether it is generated from within the person, received from outside, bestowed by God, or carried generationally — is a constitutional location question and belongs in T2. The analysis of why it originates there — which faculty is engaged in that origination, how it operates relationally in being received or given, what structural relationship it has with adjacent characteristics — is examined in T3, T4, and T6 respectively. T2 maps the constitutional what; the other tiers examine the why and how.*

**T3 — The Inner Faculties.** T3 examines a characteristic through the lens of the human person's active inner capacities — the faculties through which every characteristic is received, processed, expressed, and chosen. The inner faculties are not locations (T2) and are not characteristics being studied — they are the constitutional equipment the person brings to every inner-being encounter. Every characteristic engages some of these faculties and not others; the pattern of engagement is part of the characteristic's identity. The faculties T3 examines are: perception (the inner senses — Scripture evidences inner analogues to each of the five physical senses: inner hearing as spiritual receptivity — *he who has ears to hear*; inner sight as the eyes of the heart — *that the eyes of your heart may be enlightened*; inner taste as direct experiential knowledge — *taste and see that the Lord is good*; inner touch as the sense of presence and reality; inner smell as the perception of quality — *a fragrant offering*. Beyond these five, Scripture and human experience point toward a sixth faculty of perception — spiritual discernment or intuition: knowing beyond rational process, awareness that does not arrive through the five senses or through cognitive reasoning. This sixth perception is provisionally seated in the spirit level of the constitution and is held as a live question for the programme's analytical work); cognition (knowing, understanding, discerning — not housed in the brain but transcending the body); memory (the temporal depth of the inner person — holding and retrieving inner-being reality across time, distinct from cognition of the present); affect (feeling and emotional experience); creativity (the faculty of origination — encompassing imagination and the capacity to bring into being what did not exist; grounded in the image of the Creator God); volition (the God-given capacity to choose — constitutionally given, distinguishing the human person from other creatures, and operating under the constraints of DNA, formation, and circumstance); agency (the capacity to act, initiate, trigger, and make happen — distinct from volition, which precedes it); moral evaluation (the capacity to assess against a standard — right, wrong, good, true); conscience (the acute inner witness of sin, guilt, and conviction — distinct from moral evaluation as the broader faculty); conscientiousness (the integrated response of moral awareness, volition, and action); and relational capacity (the constitutional equipment for genuine connection with another person). *Scope boundary: T3 asks what inner capacities the person brings and how a characteristic engages them. It does not ask where the characteristic is constitutionally located (T2), how it operates across relational interfaces (T4), or how it develops the person over time (T5).*

**T4 — Relational Interfaces.** T4 examines how a characteristic operates across the three relational interfaces of the human person — with God, with other humans, and with other spiritual beings. The governing question names relational interfaces explicitly: the human person exists in structured relationship — not as an isolated individual but as a being constitutionally oriented toward God, other humans, and the wider spiritual reality. Every inner-being characteristic has some operation across these interfaces — it is received through them, expressed through them, shaped by them, or shapes them. **The divine interface** examines the characteristic in the God-to-human and human-to-God directions: what it reveals about God's disposition toward the human person, the basis on which God extends or withholds it, and how the person seeks, receives, and responds to it in worship, supplication, and covenant. **The human interface** examines how the characteristic operates between persons: whether and how the person who has received it extends it to others, what relational orientations enable or block its extension, and whether it operates differently within existing relationships versus across relational boundaries. **The spiritual beings interface** examines the characteristic's operation in relation to other spiritual beings — both angelic and adversarial. Scripture is explicit that the human person inhabits a wider spiritual environment populated by beings other than God and other humans: angels who serve and communicate, and adversarial spiritual powers who oppose, tempt, accuse, and oppress. Every inner-being characteristic exists within this wider spiritual environment. Some characteristics are explicitly shaped by encounter with spiritual beings — fear in the presence of an angel, deception by an adversarial spirit, strengthening through angelic ministry. Others are the terrain on which adversarial spiritual activity operates — the mind as the field of deceptive thought, the conscience as the site of accusation and counter-accusation. T4 asks whether this characteristic has a named relationship to the spiritual beings interface in Scripture, and what that relationship reveals. This interface is currently underrepresented in the observation question catalogue — the programme recognises this as a gap and will address it as the analytical framework develops. *Scope boundary: T4 asks how a characteristic operates across relational interfaces. It does not ask where it is constitutionally located (T2), through which inner faculties it operates (T3), or how it develops the person over time (T5).*

**T5 — Formative and Developmental Dimension.** T5 examines how a characteristic shapes the person over time — what it does to the person across time, through what process and mechanism, in what direction, and toward what ultimate end. T5 is distinct from T3 (which asks what inner capacities are engaged) and T4 (which asks how the characteristic operates relationally). T5 asks about the developmental arc — the person before, during, and after the characteristic has done its formative work. T5 examines the nature of the transformation the characteristic produces — whether it changes the person's condition or the person's orientation to their condition. It examines the sequence of inner states through which the characteristic moves the person, and the mechanism of change — whether through discipline, transformation, encounter, or something else. It examines the relationship between the characteristic and suffering and affliction as formative contexts. It examines how the characteristic shapes the person in the longer arc of formation and sanctification. And it examines the eschatological trajectory — the ultimate direction the characteristic points toward, and what its present experience anticipates about a future fullness. The constitutional deposit question from T2 feeds into T5: where T2 identifies that sustained operation of a characteristic leaves a constitutional deposit in the body or its design, T5 examines the developmental consequence of that deposit — what it produces in the person over time, and in those who come after. *Scope boundary: T5 asks how a characteristic shapes the person over time. It does not ask where it is constitutionally located (T2), through which faculties it operates (T3), or how it connects to other characteristics (T6).*

**T6 — Structural Relationships with Other Characteristics.** T6 maps a characteristic within the wider landscape of the inner person — identifying connections, dependencies, sequences, overlaps, and distinctions with other characteristics. The governing question names the mapping of interrelationships as a programme purpose. No characteristic exists in isolation. Every characteristic has structural relationships — some characteristics precede others, some produce others, some exclude others, some co-occur consistently, some share vocabulary at the root level. T6 makes these relationships visible and examined. T6 examines co-occurrence patterns (which adjacent characteristics appear most frequently in the same verses), sequential relationships (which characteristics precede, follow, or accompany this one), causal and constitutive relationships (whether this characteristic produces another or is produced by one), vocabulary and root sharing (which adjacent characteristics share terms or root architecture), distinctions (where apparent overlap between characteristics requires careful differentiation), shared verse anchors (where a verse functions as a primary anchor in more than one characteristic's study), and dimensional sharing (how many of this characteristic's confirmed dimensions are shared with another). *Scope boundary: T6 asks how this characteristic relates structurally to other characteristics. It does not ask how it operates within the person (T2, T3) or how it develops the person over time (T5).*

**T7 — Evidential and Methodological Foundation.** T7 defines where the knowledge of a characteristic comes from and how it is derived with integrity. It is the epistemological basis that underlies all other tiers. T7 is qualitatively different from T0–T6. The other tiers define the body of understanding — the substantive areas that together constitute a complete characterisation. T7 defines the epistemological foundation — the sources and disciplines from which understanding in every other tier is derived and validated. T7 does not stand alongside the other tiers as a peer analytical area; it underlies all of them. T7 has three components. **Lexical and semantic analysis** covers the original language vocabulary of the characteristic — Hebrew and Greek terms, root meanings, grammatical forms, semantic range, canonical development across the Testaments, LXX bridging, and NT coinage. This is the primary linguistic evidence base from which all findings across every tier are drawn. **Verse and literary interpretation** covers how the characteristic functions within its verse evidence — the word's role in the sentence, the logical structure of the argument, the literary form (narrative, psalm, prophecy, wisdom, epistle), and the contextual setting (judicial, liturgical, covenantal, communal, eschatological). **Human science frameworks** covers the interpretive lenses drawn from psychology, moral philosophy, developmental psychology, sociology, anthropology, and related disciplines — applied as sanity checks to ensure coherence and completeness, not as co-equal sources alongside Scripture. *Scope boundary: T7 is the evidential and methodological foundation. It underlies all other tiers. It does not itself produce substantive findings about a characteristic — it validates and grounds the findings produced by T0–T6.*
record.heading: The Observations Framework — First Tier
record.author: researcher

record.body:
Before any word could be examined, a prior question had to be settled: what is being studied when Scripture's "inner-being" vocabulary is read word by word? The answer is the programme's working definition of inner-being characteristics — a single sentence, carefully composed, precise enough to test any English word for inclusion in the scope, broad enough to capture the full range of what Scripture describes.

**The definition.** *Inner-being characteristics are the non-physical, internal states, capacities, and expressions that constitute a person's invisible life — encompassing how a person thinks, feels, chooses, relates, and orients themselves toward meaning, others, and God.*

This is a working definition, not a theological statement. Theological accounts of the soul and spirit have been abundantly written; this programme does not add another to the list. What the programme needed instead was an evaluative filter: a formula that could be applied to any word in the English language and return a reliable yes-or-no on whether its meaning qualifies as inner-being content. The definition is that filter.

Three decisions are embedded in the definition and govern how it is applied. First, the *non-physical* test: bodily processes, external behaviours, and material realities do not qualify unless they are used to express an internal state. Weeping qualifies when it is Scripture's language for inner grief; walking does not qualify when it is only physical locomotion. Second, the *internal* test: states that originate within the person — capacities, dispositions, operations of mind and heart. The boundary here is porous because inner states can be caused by external agents, including God, other people, and spiritual forces, and the programme's analysis expects and examines that permeability. Third, the *operational range* — thinks, feels, chooses, relates, orients — which names the full working field of the inner person. These are not five sealed domains but five dimensions of a single integrated life.

The definition deliberately holds spirit and soul together under the term "inner being". Inner being is the totality of the person's non-physical existence — everything that is not the body, encompassing spirit and soul together. Soulish characteristics are a subset of that totality — the specific functions and expressions that belong to the *psyche / nephesh*: thought, emotion, will, desire, conscience, self-awareness. All soulish characteristics are inner-being characteristics; not all inner-being characteristics are soulish. The spiritual dimension — the person's orientation toward God, the capacity for divine encounter, the operations of the spirit — belongs to the inner being without being reducible to soul function. Whether a given word belongs primarily to the soul domain, primarily to the spirit domain, or to the boundary between them is one of the research questions the programme is designed to answer — not a premise it brings to the text.

A governing rule of application extends the definition's reach. Borderline words are included, not excluded. Where a word sits close to the edge of the definition, the programme includes it and flags the borderline status for later review. The cost of over-inclusion is visible and recoverable; the cost of silent omission is invisible and not recoverable. Completeness is chosen over tidiness, and the filter errs on the side of admitting words that may later be ruled out rather than excluding words that should have been ruled in.
record.heading: Defining Inner Being
record.author: researcher

record.body:
The subject this programme investigates — the human inner being — is not studied only by Scripture. Neuroscience, psychology, physiology, behavioural science, and other empirical fields examine the same territory from a different direction. The programme holds both accounts open, not by accident and not as a concession, but as a deliberate methodological stance: Scripture and science together provide a fuller picture of the human person than either one produces on its own.

The two accounts are not of equal weight in this programme. Scripture is the primary lens; science is the second lens. Framework B is biblical research — its primary data is the biblical text, its primary method is lexical and contextual analysis, its conclusions are grounded in and accountable to what Scripture says. The scientific literature is engaged to illuminate, ground, and sometimes challenge the biblical account, not to generate an independent parallel dataset of equal authority. The distinction matters because a co-equal scientific programme would require a second corpus-level effort as large as the biblical one; a second-lens engagement requires disciplined, targeted use of what science has already established.

Each lens provides what the other cannot. Scripture carries the theological frame that science has no instrument for: the human being created by God, bearing the divine image, corrupted by sin, being renewed by the Spirit. Scripture names the divine dimension — God as active agent within the inner life, who causes, sustains, judges, and transforms inner states. Scripture speaks of realities that empirical observation cannot reach: conscience, worship, the fear of the Lord, the operations of the Spirit, spiritual oppression and freedom. Science, for its part, provides empirical grounding — the observable expressions, biological substrates, and measurable patterns of inner life. Science describes how inner states are implemented in the body: the neurochemistry of fear, the physiology of grief, the neural correlates of shame, the brain-body systems through which cognition and emotion operate. Science offers phenomenological depth on what inner states feel like, how they develop, and what conditions produce or diminish them. And science provides a contemporary bridge: the programme's findings need to be readable by people living now, and scientific grounding gives them traction in present conversation.

Where the two accounts converge, the convergence is significant — two very different instruments pointing at the same reality. Where they diverge, the divergence is equally significant and is named rather than papered over. The programme identifies three kinds of convergence — phenomenological (the same experience described from different angles), mechanistic (science describing the how of what Scripture describes as a reality), and structural (the architecture of the inner life having the same shape in both accounts). It identifies three kinds of divergence — register divergence (the accounts addressing different levels of the same reality and only appearing to conflict), reductive divergence (a scientific account that loses dimensions the biblical account treats as primary), and genuine divergence (claims in actual tension that cannot be harmonised by reframing). The discipline is honest engagement, not forced harmonisation.

Three principles govern the interaction of the two lenses. Scripture is not subordinate to science, and science is not subordinate to Scripture; they are different instruments addressing different aspects of the same reality, and neither should be forced into the other's register. The scientific account addresses the creaturely dimension of the inner being — what can be observed, measured, described from outside — while the biblical account addresses the full dimension, including the theological and spiritual realities that are invisible to empirical observation. The goal is not harmonisation but honest engagement: where science says something the biblical account does not address, the observation is noted; where science says something that appears to contradict the biblical account, the apparent contradiction is examined carefully rather than quickly resolved in either direction.
record.heading: Science and the Bible
record.author: researcher

record.body:
Success for this programme has a definite shape. At the level of the individual word, it is a written study that treats the word on its own terms — what the term means across its Hebrew and Greek originals, how its occurrences distribute across Scripture, what contexts and characteristics the verses reveal, how the term engages the spirit-soul-body continuum, how the biblical account and the relevant scientific literature relate at the point this word occupies. The study stands on its own: a reader encountering a single word study gains a considered account of that aspect of the inner being, grounded in the evidence and transparent about what remains uncertain.

At the level of the corpus, success is the accumulation of these studies into a set that covers the inner-being vocabulary comprehensively, together with the cross-word syntheses that become possible only once the individual work is complete. When a word has been studied, its relationship to adjacent words — the ones it overlaps with, the ones it opposes, the ones that cause or are caused by it — becomes newly visible. When groups of words have been studied, patterns across the vocabulary emerge: clusters of related characteristics, recurrent structural features, places where two concepts turn out to be different angles on a single reality or where one concept splits into two that had been wrongly conflated. These syntheses are not added on top of the word studies; they are latent in them, and cross-registry analysis is the instrument that surfaces them.

At the level of the programme as a whole, success is a sustained and defensible account of the human inner being as Scripture reveals it — assembled from the bottom up, word by word, on the evidence of the biblical text, in honest engagement with what contemporary science observes of the same territory. Such an account is not the final word on any of its subjects; no such word is achievable from inside a research programme. It is, rather, a careful description that is accountable to the evidence it is built on, open about its boundary cases and unresolved questions, and structured so that subsequent work — the researcher's or another's — can extend or correct it from the same base.

The programme's audience is not primarily academic, though the work should be defensible in an academic setting. The intended readers are people who care about the subject — teachers, practitioners, thoughtful readers who have encountered Scripture's vocabulary of the inner life and want a careful treatment of it. The work is written for them: theologically serious without being technical for its own sake, empirically grounded without being reductively scientific, slow enough to treat its subject with respect, structured enough to be navigated rather than merely read through.

The programme will be judged a success if three things are true of its completed output. First, the account it produces is demonstrably grounded in the evidence — every substantive claim can be traced back to the verses, terms, and contextual patterns that produced it. Second, the account is open where the evidence is open — unresolved questions are named as unresolved, inferences are labelled as inferences, and the reader is trusted to work with provisional findings rather than protected from them. Third, the account is useful — it changes how someone reading it thinks about the subject, gives them vocabulary and distinctions they did not previously have, and equips them to read Scripture's inner-being texts with sharper attention.
record.heading: Expected Outcome
record.author: researcher
